newsitem.title: USA: CBOT corn ends higher on hot, dry weather outlook.
newsitem.headline: CBOT corn ends higher on hot, dry weather outlook.

text.p: CBOT corn futures closed higher on Monday amid forecasts for another bout of hot, dry weather in the U.S. Corn Belt, pit sources said.

"The weather left something to be desired," said Vic Lespinasse, trader with Dean Witter. "We didn't get as much rain as we thought and there's very little rain in the forecast. It's going to be cooler for a few days but then it's going to heat up again toward the end of the week."
Meteorologists said weekend storms brought 0.10 to 0.50 inch with about 20 percent coverage in central Illinois. The trade had expected heavier rainfall and wider coverage.
Weather Services Corp meteorologist Mike Palmerino said hot, dry weather would return by next weekend.
"The heat may persist," he said. "This one doesn't look like the heat will break all that quickly. Above normal temperatures may continue into next week."
Corn ended 8-3/4 to 2-1/2 cents per bushel higher with December up 8-3/4 at $2.52.

Trade sources noted that CBOT Illinois Corn Yield futures closed down three bushels per acre to 140 bushels, while the U.S. Corn Yield fell by one bushel to 133. Those contracts are seen as barometers of trade expectations on yield.

Traders said the drop in the Yield contracts was linked to last weekend's hot weather as well as the forecasts. Last weekend was the hottest so far this year for the Corn Belt with temperatures topping 95 degrees Fahrenheit in much of the central U.S. Midwest.
But rainfall amounts late Sunday and early Monday were less than expected. Hot, dry weather can stress the corn crop during pollination.
Peoria, Ill., had received 0.91 inch over the last 30 days. That was 23 percent of normal. Springfield, Ill., had received 1.18 inches, or 34 percent or normal.
"The rains came into western Illinois and just died," said Fred Gesser, chief forecaster with Weather Express Inc in Nebraska.

After the close of trading, USDA said 68 percent of the corn crop was in good to excellent condition, unchanged from the previous week. Many trade sources had anticipated an improvement in crop ratings after last week's rains.
Traders also focused on hot weather in northern China where sources said the crop had suffered substantial losses.
Smith Barney meteorologist Jon Davis said last week brought more hot, dry weather.
"There is no question that there have been substantial declines in yield potential for the corn crop in these areas," he said of China.
USDA export inspections data was termed mildly supportive. USDA on Monday said 27,180,000 bushels of corn were inspected for export in the week ended July 24, up from 22,943 the previous week.

There was also talk Taiwan would tender for U.S. corn and Japan was seen stepping up U.S. corn purchases ahead of the mid-August holiday season. Trade sources said Japan had covered up to 30 percent of its U.S. corn needs for the last quarter of 1997.

On the day, funds bought at least 12 million bushels, led by Refco Inc with four million bushels December, two million September and one million March bought, pit sources said. Griffin Trading bought four million December while Cargill Inc and Prudential Securities each bought two million September and December.

In options, Refco sold 400 December $2.40 puts at 7-3/4 cents, Smith Barney bought 400 December $2.30 puts at four cents and Prudential Securities bought 400 September $2.60 calls at four to 4-1/4 cents.
Volatility in the September closed at 27-1/2 percent.
Corn futures volume was estimated by CBOT at 60,000 contracts, compared with Friday's actual volume of 31,534 contracts. Options volume was pegged at 20,000, against Friday's actual of 14,110.
